Wednesday, October 31, 1923. The Right Hon. Charles Stewart, M.P., Minister of the Interior,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Mr. Stewart,
Reference is requested to my letter of October 16, 1922. Since that time my progress lias been delayed by a continuation of the combination of circumstances therein depicted.
The plant was brought into operation in September 1922 and owing to faulty material provided for the packing of the joints, experienced a disastrous fire. Repairs were made and the plant brought into operation again. As was only to be expected, numerous defects were found both in the plant and the operation of the process. Therefore the operation of the experimental plant for the past year has resolved itself into the carrying out of test runs for short periods and the shutting down for relatively long periods for the design of new apparatus, placing of contract for the construction of new equipment, alterations and repairs. Costly delays have occurred, due to strikes and the bad labour conditions existing in this country generally, and in this part of the country particularly. The main delays have been due, firstly to a prolonged local strike in the works where we are operating, and secondly, to the failure of contractors to live up to their contracts and deliver materials as and when agreed. The difficulty of carrying to a conclusion under the trade and labour conditions existing in this country a proposal of this nature can hardly be realized by anyone who has not attempted it here.
Notwithstanding these handicaps, very considerable progress has been made in the
solution of the problem. It has not been solved, but we feel we are very near it. and my experts advise me the difficulties are not chemical but are purely mechanical. The work has been very costly, and our expenditure for the past year has been approximately $85,000.00. As soon as the books have been audited a certificate from Sir W. B. Peat & Co., our auditors, will be forwarded.
Mr. Charles Camsell, Deputy Minister of Mines, visited the plant in operation last week and will no doubt report to you upon the subject of the results achieved to date.
I would respectfully call your attention to the adverse change in the situation, as regards the establishment of a commercial plant for the development of tar sands at the present time, due to the over-production in California and the consequent slump in all oil propositions.
Under the circumstance noted above it is respectfully requested
(a)	that I may be granted an extension of one year from November 30, 1923, for time within which to erect a commercial plant in the McMurray district.
(b)	that the large expenditure already incurred-as certified by Sir W. B. Peat & Co. up to July 31, 1922, and to be certified by them for the past year-be accepted in lieu of rentals for the next year.
In connection therewith reference is made to your letter of January 4, 1923, and favourable consideration is requested.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd) W. Bethune Lindsay.

Memorandum
Re: General Lindsay's Plant for the treatment of bituminous sands.
This plant is situated near Swansea, South Wales, and was visited by me in September 1922. A memorandum embodying my observations of the operation of the plant was submitted to the Minister on September 28 on my return to Ottawa last year.
I visited the plant again this year on October 27 in company with General Lindsay and in reply to a request for information cabled Mr. Cory on October 29 as follows:
"Saw Lindsay's plant Saturday. No progress made on tar sand separation since last year but has concentrated on new method of refining oil. Cannot say if treatment of sands will be successful."
Questions

This cable requires elaboration in order that the situation may be clearly understood.
The process being tried out by General Lindsay consists of two operations namely: (1) the separation of the bitumen from the sand, and (2) distillation of the bitumen and separation into its different fractions by an entirely new method.
Both operations are carried out with superheated steam at high temperatures and under considerable pressure. The oil is vaporized with the steam and when the temperature is lowered condensation takes place of one fraction after another, the heavier first of all and the lighter fraction last. In this respect it is a reversal of the ordinary process of destructive distillation now used.
When the process was first tried out in this plant in September 1922, the packing and joints in the pipes were found to be incapable of withstanding the temperatures and pressures developed and a serious fire broke out, which caused a long delay.
As stated in a previous memorandum of mine on the subject of these bituminous sands, the question of distillation of the oil obtained presents many difficulties and is still an unsolved problem. Lindsay claims that his process of distillation, when perfected, will solve this problem, but of that I cannot speak authoritatively. In consequence of this he has devoted all his attention during the last year to perfecting his process of distillation, and there is no doubt he has made very good progress and appears to be within sight of success.
For this operation he has been using crude oil supplied him by the Auglo-Persian Oil Co., and has been putting through the plant an amount ranging from 150 to 300 barrels a day. His plant has a maximum capacity of about 500 gallons per hour.
He claims to have done sufficient work on the separation of the oil from our sands to feel that his process will perform this operation successfully, but he argues that he dare not use up the 40 tons of sand supplied him until he has the second and more important operation of distillation completely worked out. Looking at the whole process broadly I think he is quite right in this respect.
There is no doubt that the cost of these experiments have run into a great deal of money, and he states that he has expended during the last year some $S5,000. An audit of his books will be made by Sir W. B. Peat & Company and a copy of this furnished to the Department of the Interior.
Charles Camsell,
Deputy Minister of Mines.

Dear Mr. Stewart,-
With reference to my recent application for permission to alter the selections of tar sand areas originally made by me to others which explorations completed since that time, have indicated to be more desirable, I feel it may be useful if I advise you of the conclusions I have reached after a further study of the situation as regards the development of these tar sand areas.
Until oil can be produced from tar sands and sold in competition with oil derived from wells it does not appear to be feasible to develop these deposits economically. The present tremendous excess production of oil in California has necessarily retarded this. It will be recognized that it is hardly practicable to induce capital to enter this field until assured of a successful process, leases which can be developed profitably and a reasonable market for their products. All of this will take time.
My original selection was based on imperfect data available in 1920. This information has been, I understand, largely supplemented by new exploration work but the results will hardly be available for some time.
The original selections consisted of, if I remember correctly, something like 16 blocks. At the request of the Department this was reduced in 1922 to 9 blocks. In accordance with the last request of the department the section has been still further reduced to 4 main blocks and one small block near Mac-Murray, which is necessary, on account of its situation, for the preliminary work on a small scale.
I	feel however that the potential effect of this arbitrary reduction in number and location of leases is not fully realized for the following reasons:-
(1)	Surface indications are very unreliable as to the value of a lease. While I understand a great deal of information has been collected regarding surface indications, this will not be available for a long time. No information is available as to the depth or nature of over-burden, the continuity of deposits, or the value of deposits. A glance at the diagram given below will make this clear.
(Diagram).
(2)	Under these circumstances a company might expend a large sum of money in the development of a successful process and find

Questions
they had leases which could not be operated successfully. I may, therefore, have discarded leases of greater value than those now applied for.
(3) The value of these deposits cannot be determined until they are prospected by coredrilling. As far as I know there is no coredrill as yet available which will operate successfully on these deposits.
In view of the large sums of money already expended by us and the fact that I was the first to take up this question, I feel that it is only reasonable that:-
(a)	The selections now made should be considered provisional;
(b)	If the detailed exploration work planned for the future discloses better tar sand areas,
I	should be accorded permission to change and priority of selection.
(c)	Every help should be given to ensure exploration and prospecting by core-drilling.
It is understood that some of the areas recently prospected and considered of value have not yet been placed within the tar sand reserve. It is respectfully suggested that this should be done as the information is gathered.
Thanking you in anticipation, believe me, sir,
Yours very truly,
W. Bethune Lindsay.

Report Respecting Experimental Plant for
Treatment of Bituminous Sands and Refining of Oils Erected and Operated under the
Direction of General W. B. Lindsay at
Landarcy, Near Swansea, South Wales.
This Plant was visited by Dr. Charles Camsell, deputy Minister of Mines, in September 1922. and again in October 1923, and reports were submitted thereon to the minister on September 28, 1922, and November 1923.
Pursuant to the request that a further report be made in the matter as to the progress that had been made in these investigations since Dr. Camsell's visit to Swansea in October 1923 the undersigned met General Lindsay in London on two occasions September 4th and October 1st and in addition visited the experimental plant at Landarcy near Swansea, South Wales, on Thursday, September 24th. 1925, in company with Mr. Herbert W. Wagner, who had been Technical Engineer in charge of operations under General Lindsay.
The experimental work on the refining of Persian crude oil referred to by Dr. Camsell
in his report dated November 30, 1923, was continued till June 1924, at which time, owing to the exhaustion of available funds, experimental operation of the plant ceased, and has not since been resumed. It may be inferred from the mass of detailed records of the experimental work done, that good progress had been made in improving the plant operation and in gradually securing better and better results in respect to the refined products secured; though for final demonstration it appeared desirable to try some further additions to the plant which, while simple in principle, would be quite expensive to install.
Unfortunately General Lindsay and his associates have been having difficulty in securing United States patents, and the delay in securing these, it is claimed, is militating against the immediate securing of further capital for experimental work.
In the meantime Mr. Herbert W. Wagner is undertaking some small scale laboratory investigations at Cardiff on the oils actually derived from the bituminous sands, a small portion of the 40 tons of bituminous sand originally sent to Swansea having been transferred to Cardiff for that purpose. This work had been in progress a few months only at the time of my visit.
In reviewing the work that has been done by General Lindsay to demonstrate the Cafftoo process and its applicability to the treatment of Alberta bituminous sands, the following appear to the undersigned as being important points:-
1.	The experimental plant at Landarcy which is on the property of the Anglo-Persian oil company, is on a substantial scale requiring a throughput of from 150 to 300 barrels of oil per day for its operation.
2.	No actual tests of bituminous sands have been made in this plant for the reason that it would be impractical to supply a sufficient quantity of the sand for that purpose. The quantity of 40 tons supplied for experimental use would be used up in a few hours, and would not supply a sufficient quantity of oil for practical test in the plant.
3.	General Lindsay is strongly of the opinion that if he can- successfully demonstrate the application of the Cafftoo process to the refining of such oils as persian crude,, he will have comparatively little difficulty in adapting the process to the treatment of the bituminous sands. On this latter assumption 1 am not prepared to offer an opinion.
4.	Assuming the successful demonstration of the Cafftoo process for the treatment of persian crude oil, another experimental plant would require to be constructed at a point
Questions

convenient to an adequate supply of bituminous sand in order that a full demonstration could be made in respect to the treatment of such sands.
5.	Prior to June 1924, a very large amount of money-the evidence in respect to which is, I believe, already on file with the interior department-has been expended in the effort to solve the problem of the treatment of the tar sands.
6.	Actual experimental work at Landarcy ceased in June 1924.
7.	General Lindsay is endeavouring to enlist further capital in the project, but is being delayed through difficulty in securing U.S. patents
Respectfully submitted,

1.	Is there an inventions board or committee within the government of Canada? If so, what are the names of the members, and who is the chairman?
2.	How many inventions or suggestions have been made to this board since the commencement of the war?
3.	How many have been accepted as useful and are at the present time being put to use?
4.	When inventions or suggestions are received by the board, what is the procedure in dealing with them?

1.	Yes. There is an inventions board composed of the president, national research council, chairman; a deputy minister of national defence (army); the deputy minister of national defence (air); the deputy minister for naval services; and Mr. Lesslie R. Thomson of the Department of Munitions and Supply who is secretary of the board.
2.	13.548.
3.	Precise numbers are not available. About four-fifths of the proposals received deal with ideas which have been previously considered by the board or that are of slight technical interest but no military value. About ten per cent of the proposals have some evident merit which warrants reference being made to military consultants. Data as to the number of these actually put into use cannot be released.
4.	All inventions and suggestions received by the board go in the first instance to one of four sub-committees of the board. These primary committees are the civilian consulting committee, the army consulting committee, the naval consulting committee, and the air force consulting committee. The duties of these sub-committees are to receive and to screen all suggestions and inventions received from
fMr. Crerar.]
the sources which their respective names indicate. Upon receipt of any suggestion or invention an acknowledgment is immediately sent to the inventor to thank him. The suggestion or invention is then referred to the appropriate technical consultants within either the armed services or the national research council. Occasionally other consultants are used. Upon receipt of the technical consultants' reports, a letter is then sent to the-inventor setting out the essence of what has been ascertained. If the suggestion has been appraised as of no value, the author is so informed. If the suggestion is useful but refers only to administrative improvements and the like within any one of the services, the consulting committee of that service deals finally with the suggestion. If, on the other hand, the proposal has been appraised as useful in itself but of no particular value to the war effort, permission is likely to be given by the inventions board to the inventor to exploit the particular invention to his own advantage. If the invention or suggestion is believed to be of value to the war effort, the matter is then referred to the board's main examining committee which meets monthly, and makes recommendations to the board regarding patent application, further development work, or other courses of action.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Importations of grapefruit
juice were declared ineligible for subsidy consideration as of May 11, 1942. As the price of grapefruit juice has increased sharply in the United States since the inception of the price ceiling, importation by private concerns for sale at domestic ceiling prices is virtually impossible.
However, under the authority of a minute of the wartime prices and trade board, dated June 16. 1942, the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation Limited bulk purchased grapefruit juice to meet the requirements of the Department of Munitions and Supply, and a further minute of the board, dated August 25, 1942, authorized the corporation to purchase a specified quantity for the Canadian Red Cross Society. Sales to these purchasers are at cost, therefore no trading loss is incurred.
In the fall of 1943, due to the fact that a large percentage (38 per cent) of the 1943 pack of tomato juice was to be retained for priority claimants, and there was an anticipated shortage of tomato juice for civilian users, it appeared advisable to make available a supply of grapefruit juice.
There had been, in the United States, a release of 2,700,000 cases of 1942 pack for civilian use, together with an additional supply of approximately 3,000,000 cases of 1943 pack over and above the 1942 pack. This increased the availability of the commodity, and on November 9, 1943. wartime prices and trade board authorized Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation Ltd., to bulk purchase for resale, grapefruit juice for civilian consumption in Canada.
In order that grapefruit juice may be sold in compliance with the maximum prices regulations, the corporations selling prices are necessarily below cost. On total purchases of some 700,000 cases the trading loss is expected to be approximately 81 per case, but it is felt that the nutritional value and high Vitamin C content, so necessary to the Canadian diet, justify the cost to the government.
The corporations purchases are distributed through the normal trade channels on the basis of the importers' 1941-42 average purchases. Shipments are made against the allocations of the administrator of imported grocery items of the wartime prices and trade board, who has completed arrangements with the Food brokers association for equitable distribution throughout Canada. For the corporations actual selling prices to the first distributor, reference may be made to administrator's order A-1073. In the case of U.S. grapefruit juice, prices are f.o.b. U.S. shipping point, actual importation being completed by _ the first distributor. In the case of Trinidad grapefruit juice, prices are on a delivered basis at central distributing points in the maritime provinces.

What steps, if any, is the administration taking to relieve the radio tube shortage in this country?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The production of radio
tubes is under the Department of Munitions and Supply, therefore most of the Canadian production of tubes is necessarily absorbed by the radio and radar requirements of the armed services.
The only supply of tubes which can be made available for civilian use arises from those which can be produced over and above the requirements of the services.
The same shortage of radio tubes prevails in the United States, but through arrangements made between the war production board and the wartime prices and trade board, a normal share of the American production is being secured for Canadian users.
It is also hoped that during the last half of this current year, increased supplies will be available from the Canadian manufacturers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Under present regulations a farmer in Manitoba may have his cattle and hogs killed for him at a government inspected abattoir (but there is no obligation on the abattoir to do such slaughtering unless it was customarily engaged in such business in the year of 1941). The resultant meat may be sold by the farmer to neighbour farmers and to household consumers, but not to anyone else, unless the farmer is the holder of a slaughtering permit issued by the wartime prices and trade board or unless his farm is located in a deficiency production area in Manitoba which is defined as follows: "All territory north of the 53rd parallel".

speechtext:
I have a question I desire to direct to the acting leader of the government. I understand that a committee representing various departments of government has been constituted to deal with Canadian trade arrangements. If such a committee has been set up by the government, by what name will it be designated, what will be its functions, who will be its chairman and who will comprise its personnel?
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs): May I be permitted to answer the question? On April 27

External Trade
last there was adopted on the recommendation of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie King) an order in council setting up an interdepartmental committee which will be known as the external trade advisory committee. It was represented that the war has reached a stage at which prompt decisions have to be reached on many questions of export and import trade policy which concern several departments and agencies of government, particularly in relation to their effect upon the volume of supplies available for Canadian civilian or military use, or for alternative urgent external requirements, including relief and rehabilitation. It was thought desirable that an agency should be established for prompt consultation between departments and other agencies of government on such matters.
The membership of the committee is to consist of persons to be nominated as follows: One member by the Secretary of State for External Affairs; one member by the Minister of Trade and Commerce; one member by the Minister of Munitions and Supply, to represent the Department of Munitions and Supply; one member by the chairman of the mutual aid board, to represent the administration of that board; one member by the Minister of Finance to represent the Department of Finance; one member by the Minister of Finance to represent the wartime prices and trade board, and a third member by the Minister of Finance, to represent the foreign exchange control board; one member by the Minister of National Revenue, and one member by the Minister of Agriculture.
The functions of this committee are: (a) to serve as a medium for consultation between departments and agencies of government on questions concerning export and import trade; (b) to make recommendations and reports to ministers, departments or agencies of the government on matters relating to wartime export and import trade, or to trade during the period of transition to peace; (c) in appropriate cases to refer questions bearing upon import or export trade to other interdepartmental committees or boards for consideration; (d) to investigate matters concerning export or import trade in war time or in the period of transition to peace, and to obtain information thereon from departments and agencies of the government; (e) without restricting the generality of the foregoing, to investigate, consider and make recommendations concerning the supplying by Canada of goods and services for relief and rehabilitation purposes.
The members of the committee have been appointed. I shall lay on the table a copy of the order in council, which is being published
in the publication containing such orders in council; and annexed to it is a list of the persons appointed to the committee and of alternates to act in their absence.
The committee had a meeting on the second instant, and Mr. Sydney Pierce was chosen by the members of the committee as their chairman. Mr. Pierce is the director general of the Washington office of munitions and supply, on loan to the Department of External Affairs; he was chosen by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to represent that department on the committee. The list of members of the committee and their alternates is quite long, and if I may be permitted to do so I shall table the list together with a copy of the order in council.

speechtext:
I should like to ask the Minister of Labour to give the house the present position of the labour dispute in the plant of the Ford Motor Company of Canada Limited at Windsor, and also to indicate the steps
Labour-Ford Motor Company

the government is taking to ensure a settlement of this dispute in order that war production may be resumed.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: DISPUTE AT THE PLANT OF FORD MOTOR COMPANY
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition was good enough to give me notice of this question, and I should like to make the following statement. The Ford Motor Company of Canada Limited, Windsor, Ontario, had contractual relations with local No. 200 of the United Automobile Workers of America. The two parties signed an agreement in December, 1942, and renewed it with some slight changes, in January, 1944. Under this agreement provision was made for a procedure whereby stewards would handle and investigate grievances. This procedure specified that stewards night leave their regular duties for a reasonable length of time, subject to the approval of their foremen and subject also to a maximum absence from their regular duties of two hours per working day and not more than three hours in any two consecutive working days. However, if the foreman was of the opinion that more than a reasonable period of time had been taken by a steward he could decline to approve payment to the steward for such excess time.
It was the contention of the union that a practice had arisen over the last two years under which stewards serviced grievances without any of these restrictions and because the company decided to adhere to the written terms of the contract representations were made do the wartime labour relations board, that is the national board, for an interpretation or clarification of the grievance procedure in the light of the current practice. The board had arranged to hear the parties on April 25, but in the meantime the company issued misconduct slips to stewards who were considered to be violating the terms of the agreement. Later four stewards were suspended for six days, and this culminated in a stoppage of work on April 20. There was a clause in the agreement which provided that if a strike occurred the agreement could be terminated immediately, and pursuant to this provision immediately the stoppage took place the company served notice on the union that it considered the agreement at an end.
The	wartime	labour relations board(national) invited representatives	of	thecompany and the union to Ottawa, and for four days last week made an effort to conciliate the dispute. On Saturday the company and the union accepted a proposal drafted by the board. It was an important condition of the proposal that the wartime labour relations board	(national)	would determine	the	procedure	applying	to representation	and	the
tMr. Graydon.]
settlement of grievances for the period during which the parties would be in negotiation for a new contract, and that in the event of a dispute as to the interpretation or application of the provisions of the settlement or of the grievance procedure established by the board, it would be submitted to arbitration under the direction of the board.
The board submitted the grievance procedure to both parties on Monday of this week and immediately appointed one of the senior conciliating officers of the Department of Labour as an interim impartial umpire to facilitate the application of the grievance procedure and the final adjustment of disputes arising in connection therewith, his decision-and this was agreed to-to be final and binding on both parties. On Tuesday, May 2, it developed that the union objected to the grievance procedure as laid down by the board and at a mass meeting decided on a further stoppage of work which became effective at midnight of that date. According to newspaper reports the decision of the union to strike on midnight of May 2 was taken against the advice of the president of local No. 200 of the union, Mr. Roy England, and of the Canadian director of the union, Mr. George Burt. Two of the experienced officers of the department are now on the ground and are in contact with representatives of the company and the union.

speechtext:
I should like to direct a question
to the Minister of Munitions and Supply of which I sent him notice a couple of days ago. On March 21, when the minister presented his estimates to the house, he announced the appointment of a royal commission to inquire into the coal industry, with the end in view of mapping out a post-war fuel policy. I should like to direct a further
question to the Minister of Labour. An Associated Press dispatch, bearing a Philadelphia dateline of yesterday, states that Sir Walter Citrine, internationally known labour leader, has to-day called off the world trade union conference scheduled for London in June, and the dispatch further indicates that the meeting may be held in Canada. Is the minister in a position to inform the house of the date and the place in Canada of such meeting?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: CANCELLATION OF LONDON MEETING-POSSIBILITY OF HOLDING CONFERENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
I read the news dispatch to which the leader of the opposition has referred. I think the answer is that pending events in Britain made it inadvisable for the proposed world trade union conference to be held as planned in London in June next.
Arrangements for the proposed conference are in the hands of Sir Walter Citrine, general secretary of the British Trades Union Congress, and it is apparent he feels the conference could be held more conveniently on this side of the Atlantic. That is particularly so in view of the fact that a number of delegates are now attending the International Labour Office conference at Philadelphia. I am sure everybody in Canada will be glad to have the conference meet here. No doubt Sir Walter Citrine will be making arrangements with the labour leaders in the dominion as to the time and place of the conference.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subsubtopic: CRASH OF LIBERATOR BOMBER IN MONTREAL ON APRIL 25-COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question of the Minister of National Defence for Air. What arrangements has the government been able to make to compensate relatives of those, who were killed in the aeroplane crash in Montreal? Also, what will be done for those whose homes were destroyed by fire and who, on account of the accident, are left homeless?
Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of National Defence for Air).: The hon. member for St. Ann (Mr. Healy), in whose constituency this unfortunate accident occurred, was good enough to give me notice of the question, and I have prepared an answer.
As the house is aware, a Liberator aircraft en route from Montreal Airport for delivery in the United Kingdom crashed in Montreal on 25th April, 1944, resulting in the death of a number of residents as well as the aircraft's crew and injury to persons and property.
The aircraft was under the control and direction of the Royal Air Force and the question of paying compensation for the pecuniary loss suffered as the result of the crash rests with the government of the United Kingdom and not the government of Canada.
I have been asked by the United Kingdom authorities to state that this question of compensation has been given careful and sympathetic consideration by the Air Ministry of the United Kingdom and that, without going into the question of legal liability, the ministry is anxious and is prepared to deal with this question of compensation on the same basis as would be adopted in the event of a similar accident in Canada in which an aircraft of the Royal Canadian Air Force had been involved.
In order that the United Kingdom Air Ministry may have full and complete information in each case where such pecuniary loss has been suffered, so as to assist it in determining what would be fair and reasonable compensation, and to implement its desire that compensation be dealt with as I have mentioned, the Canadian government is taking immediate action whereby those persons who have suffered pecuniary loss as a result of the accident will be able to have their claims in respect of such loss appraised on a fair and reasonable basis.
The circumstances are such as to make it desirable to have the matter dealt with with

the greatest expedition and the house may rest assured that this will be done and that every facility will be afforded those persons who have suffered pecuniary loss to have the same appraised on a fair and equitable basis.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, May 2, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

War Appropriation-Labour
National selective service programme. $11,002,429.

The only way to understand the scope of the problem of national selective service is to consider it not from an electoral viewpoint, but rather to study it objectively. The question is not that of pleasing the farmer or pleasing the army, but simply that of doing what is right, not being afraid to do so, and speaking accordingly. It will be impossible to discuss the problem of selective service so long as it is engulfed in politics, so long as it serves as a political platform for the jingoes or for those who hold the opposite view's. The question of man-power is one which concerns the future of this country to the utmost. It cannot be onesided; it must be well balanced. The Minister of Labour should be the regulator as between the requisitions of the army and the needs of industry; he should act as a pendulum. Ait no time should he be a stoker for the Department of National Defence.
It has been customary for certain club men, men who have never been in a theatre of war, men who may be graduates of military schools and possess some technical military knowledge but who have never won their spurs in a theatre of war, to say that it is a good thing to establish conscription of others for the waging of war. Conscription should, be preached only by example. I deny to any one who has not been in a theatre of war, even though he has studied in a military college and may wear a uniform, the right to uphold conscription. That is one point. I concede the right to those who have been in a theatre of war to hold the wrong view, but we have the right to discuss the matter without being told that we are what we are not.
A jingo is a -man who beats the drum, a man who thinks that all farmers should be in the army, that those who are not in the army are not doing their duty. They think that it is the duty of every man in good health and of military age to be in the army. That point of view is encouraged by talks sent over the C.B.C. at certain hours and it is encouraged also by the wartime information board and in a different way by the censorship regulations. News of what is said in the house is curtailed by the censors and does not reach the people who have a right to know what is being said in their defence.
Some half-truths are being uttered. When the Minister of Labour and his deputy wrote
to the government of Quebec that conscription would not be applied to farmers, that was true to a certain extent. It is true to a certain extent because of the fight that has been waged for the farmers by a small group of members of parliament who have the courage of their convictions and who can speak louder than any jingo can beat a drum. But it is essential that every hon. member of the committee should know what happened. If an hon. member asks the Minister of Labour to supply him with the same information that was requested by the premier of Quebec he will be told that the farmers receive special consideration from the mobilization boards. I admit that that may be true with regard to farmers who have never been in a military camp, but as soon as a man enters a military camp it is altogether different. That is why I have been asking questions about the postponements granted by mobilization boards in connection with draftees who are farmers' sons or who have worked on farms. When farmers have been in training for a month, these boards, which act under the Minister of Labour, consider it their duty to turn down most of the applications. They act simply as rubber stamps; they do not give due consideration to those farmers who are needed on the farms.
This condition dates back a long time. At one time the treatment accorded by the Quebec board to draftees who were farmers- and the same was true of other places-was rotten; it was an abomination. This condition was corrected to some extent, but many farmers who are indispensable are being sent to the training camps. The fact that they were farmers was not considered at all. As soon as these men received regimental numbers they were considered as belonging to the army and it was impossible for them to get back to the farm.
In how many cases have there been injustices? These people believed in the good faith of the government. They were at first told by every minister that the training would be for one month only. They did not ask for postponements, because they believed the statement that their training would be for one month only. The first training period began in November, 1940, an off season, and these men took the training believing they would be free for the rest of the year. Then they were called back for four months and finally had to stay there. They found it impossible to get leave after they were in the army.
I have a number of meritorious cases represented by the many files before me, some
War Appropriation-Labour

large and others not so large but just as deserving, covering men who have been placed in these camps under false pretences or because of the ignorance and stupidity of the members of the boards. Who suffers for this? In the first place it is the old father who cannot look after his farm alone, and it is also the country.
The jingo conception of conscription is that every able-bodied man should be in the army, without any consideration for the consequences of an unbalanced war effort. I will tell you, Mr. Chairman, how I would like things to work. In the first place there should be a campaign of information to educate the Canadian people and help them to understand what are the needs of this country. The farmer, the railway man, the miner, and all others who are working in essential industries should be rehabilitated in the minds of Canadian citizens who are not aware of the degree to which these occupations are essential to the state. That campaign can be carried on by the wartime information board and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. That would be much more useful than the pamphlets we receive and the little stories that are told over the C.B.C.
Next, the scissors of censorship must not be allowed to cut the reports of the two news agencies, the Canadian Press and the British-United Press but must give an opportunity to the Canadian people to inform themselves about the work that is done for them- here in this house.
Next, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Labour should be the boss of all draftees. I do not see why the Minister of National Defence is considered as holding a job more important than that of the Minister of Labour. Undoubtedly the job of the Minister of National Defence is important, but why should he have a priority over the Minister of Labour so that his requisitions for men must be filled at the expense of the lifeblood of the nation? This I cannot understand. It is a jingo policy when the Minister of Labour has to say "yes" to all the requistions which are made upon him by the Department of National Defence. The Minister of Labour has no information about the actual needs of the Department of National Defence. He has to take the word of its minister. What is the word of the Minister of National Defence? It is the sequel to the commitments he made when in London. The Minister of National Defence went to London and said: I will send you so many divisions. He has told us himself that he

sent men to Italy who were not requested by the British government. And we call that a fine gesture. But on account of that so-called fine gesture, which was probably inspired by international finance, Barclay's bank-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I know that the hon. member realizes that I wish to be very tolerant, and he has been allowed considerable latitude. We have been over three days considering this one item, and in my opinion international finance should be left out of this discussion and1 the hon. member should come down to earth and discuss the item before the committee.

Your mind is too quick, Mr. Chairman. I hope you will let me finish my argument, and then you will see that it is closely related to the item before us. However, I will leave aside international finance and all that, and say this. The Minister of National Defence has told us himself that it w-as not at the request of the British government that he sent our men to Sicily or Italy. But it is precisely on account of commitments of that kind made in the name of the Canadian people that the Minister of Labour is called upon to pay the bill by calling up Canadian citizens who would be better employed in the industries where they are working.
I want to say to the Minister of Labour, in all earnestness, I would like to see him in a position where he could decide these matters as a real minister in charge of man-power. I would like to see him able to say to a man who is needed in industry and wants to enlist: No, your place is not in the army, it is in the industry where you work, and you are helping the war effort best by continuing to work in that essential industry. But the Minister of Labour has not this information that he should have. How can he decide between the needs of the army and the needs of industry if he has no figures on the needs of industry and the needs of the army? He has no information on those needs. He receives a requisition from the Department of National Defence for ten thousand or one hundred thousand men. It is a requisition in bulk. But does the Minister of Labour know to what extent he will deprive industry of man-power which is urgently needed in industry if he fills the requisition of the Department of National Defence? He cannot know because he has not the figures. Very often I have made a test. I have asked the Department of Labour for figures that

War Appropriation-Labour
should be on the desk of the Minister of Labour and his deputy, and it was not possible for me to get those figures. It was not because they were secret. Those figures should have been there. It is essential for the Minister of Labour to have them if he is to know what is the man-power reserve, if any, in this country.
There are other jingoes who sing the same song all the time-we must get reinforcements for our troops overseas-we must have so many divisions-we must have so many recruits, so many men for reinforcements, and so on. It is very easy to say: Just disband one division and then you will have reinforcements sufficient for the others, for the time being. How can the Minister of Labour decide between the needs of the lumber industry, for instance, and the needs of the army? I say that in all earnestness and in the best possible spirit of friendship for the minister, who has my full sympathy. I think his job is an intolerable one. He is not the boss. He is like the office boy of the Minister of National Defence or a clerk of the minister. The Minister of National Defence tells him: We need ten thousand or one hundred thousand men. Then the Minister of Labour writes to the various boards and tells them: The army needs so many men, and we must get them. But what does the Minister of Labour know about the actual needs of the lumber industry or about the needs of the farmers, for example?
What is the difference? It comes back to what I said a moment ago. On the one hand there is a requisition from the Department of National Defence for a definite number of men. But agriculture is different. The farmers are scattered all over the land, and it is impossible for them all to reach the Minister of Labour and tell him of their needs of man-power as easily as his colleague the Minister of National. Defence can. What farmer in any province .sits in council with the Minister of Labour and has the opportunity to speak to him every day, as often as he wishes every day, as the Minister of National Defence has? The Minister of Labour is in an impossible position. That is why I said to the Minister of Labour the other day that he deserves the consideration and help of his colleagues-for what? For reform. We must make it easier for the Minister of Labour to do the things he should do. He should be the minister of man-power, with full authority over draftees, whether they are in uniform or not, provided they have not volunteered. He should be in a position to answer back when the Minister of National Defence makes an exorbitant demand upon him for men. Would it not be for the good of the nation were he to tell the Minister of National Defence: "Please keep quiet and I 100-IG4
will see to it, and after I have examined the situation carefully I will tell you whether I can give you the men or not"? He should not be bound to say "yes" to all the requests he receives from the Minister of National Defence; if he does, the future of this country will be unbalanced. It is simple to say these things, and it is precisely because these things are so simple that it is so hard to get them accepted.
What happens? We write to the Department of National Defence regarding the case of a farmer who is needed on the land, and what does that department answer? The answer is that the mobilization board has not granted the application of the father to have his son back with him on the farm, and the blame is put by the army on the mobilization board, which is under the Minister of Labour. That is ingratitude. The mobilization boards cater to the army and then get the cold shoulder as a reward. That is the way it is done. In most cases it is useless to bring before the mobilization board, which is under the Minister of Labour, the cases of soldiers who have already had some training and who are in the army now. It is a most difficult thing.
I will tell the minister more than that. There are some intriguers on the board, not all of them, but some of them who want advancement and who try to intrigue to place people in the army at the expense of justice, at the expense of the right application of the regulations. That is the way it is done, and I could tell him a sad story. But my idea was to try to bring the committee back to fundamentals, back to a basis of discussion which would be different from what has been heard before in certain quarters, a basis of discussion that would satisfy the minds of the people of any province in Canada, even if they do not all agree with it. That is my view.
I have spoken of the farmers. They enjoy a certain consideration because they are numerous and because in many counties the election is decided by the vote of the farmers. If I believed the farmers' sons did not deserve postponement from training or leave from the army I would never advocate their cause, but I do so because I believe they do not receive fair treatment, to which they are entitled, and they are led into error by the false statement that conscription does not apply to them. We have conscription in this country; undoubtedly so. The sons of farmers of military age who are on the farms now have not had any training; ninety-nine per cent of those who have had training for a month or two have been kept in the army. That is the difference, and to be honest with the people,

War Appropriation-Labour

to be honest with the leading citizens of any province, this is what should be said to them if they inquire for information.
And now with regard to the railway business, I shall have a lot to say later on. But there is a distinction also between draftees and volunteers. The other day the Minister of National Defence was non-committal regarding what had been said by Major General Pearkes in British Columbia. Here however I have a statement made by Brigadier Macklin in Vernon, according to a Canadian press dispatch of April 7. He blamed recruits for refusing to enlist in the active army when he spoke in favour of the sixth victory loan, and he did not give them an opportunity to walk in parade on the occasion of the loan, those who had not been willing to sign for overseas. That is a great humiliation to put on the men, because they were acting in accordance with the law. There is nothing that forces them to go overseas unless conscription for overseas is established now, and the only thing that is needed to send these men there is a stroke of the minister's pen, and he knows that very well.
What I regret very much is the fact that it is impossible to discuss these matters without being called personal or being told that we are wasting the time of the house. It is most unfortunate that we have reached the time when legitimate criticism is considered a personal insult by certain members of the cabinet. It is not a matter of personal pride; it is a question of the good of the country. Is it better to continue saying that all men of military age should be in the army, notwithstanding the needs of industry? If the majority of the house takes that view I will say nothing further about it in this chamber, though I will do so outside. On the other hand, if it is regarded as being for the good of the nation that the Minister of Labour should be the boss and should have the right to decide what shall be done by young men who are draftees, whether they should be in the army or not, that is another point that deserves the best consideration.
There should be only one boss. The Minister of Labour should no longer be the office boy of the Minister of National Defence. That is my point and I hope it will be well understood. I referred a moment ago to the differences between the mass requisitions that he gets from the Department of National Defence and the single applications that he receives from farmers with respect to their sons. How could the minister know the need of the farms in all Canada every week if the boards do not report to him the number of requisitions that have been received and how

they have been dealt with? Even then there is no organization to inform the minister about the needs of the farmers. The only thing that is done is by members of parliament who voice the protests of the farmers in this committee. I hope that all this will be taken into consideration. I am very anxious to see the reaction to a little bit of reflection and thought not only from the Minister of Labour but from all his colleagues as well in order to correct a situation that is going from bad to worse.

I do not wish to add to the difficulty of the minister and his deputies in their calculations. I wish to point out what I mentioned in the house before the present minister and his deputies were in the position they occupy to-day. When the war started in 1939 we were not ready for it. I am not very much interested in the battle of wits on mathematics that has been going on. I am interested in reading the various reports and records galore of counts made on man-power in this war. It is now getting near to Woodbine time. We are in a man-power pool that is nearly as bad as the Woodbine pool. The battle of wits has been going on. Let us get down to the facts. When war broke out we had the old system of records in the three forces. Each of the forces was running its own department, so to speak. We then came along to the time when the Minister of Agriculture was the head of the national resources department and a card system of registration was established. It took months and months to count up the results of that registration. Finally, they were all counted. What was the result? The count was carried on the way the census returns are dealt with, and it took nearly a year to get the returns. I admit it is a difficult task that the minister has undertaken and it is rather difficult to straighten it out. I sympathize with him in that respect. When the war broke out in 1939 I was asked by three or four municipalities if I could do something for them in this committe and that is the only matter I wish to raise to-day. I was asked to see if there could be some change made in the system of recording man-power. The records system was a relic of the South African war. When a man enlists he signs attestation papers. The system was just copied from the one used by the mother country in the other war. They have a similar system in Washington.
We have had numerous counts, and it has been a run-around, a merry-go-round, since the war started. It is not the fault of the present minister. He is the victim of the system. Where are these returns? I received five or six returns under the first system, the

War Appropriation-Labour
registration card affair. I received returns showing that so far as the records go they could not tell how many men enlisted from Toronto, St. Catharines or the minister's own riding of Welland. There was no place where we could get the figures. This is a changing war, Mt. Chairman. Do not forget that. The war is changing from week to week, from month to month, and from year to year. What was the result? They added certain formations. The artillery was in Winnipeg and Petawawa; the infantry were parcelled all over Canada. Then, there were different branches of the air force all over the country, with the result that the municipalities got all twisted up. You could not tell how many men came from Lake Centre; you could not tell how many men came from Orangeville, the riding of South Simcoe; the minister could not tell how many came from St. Catharines, or any centres like that. What became of all these figures on the three counts that were made? My point is this: in the victory loan campaigns they have a system whereby they can tell to-morrow the amount of money collected all over Canada to-day. It is a very good mathematical system yet we cannot do it in man-power. I do not know how they do it in the victory loan, but it is being done.
An attempt was made to enforce the registration card system. Officers in Toronto would walk along the street and ask you to show your card. The municipalities are helping the minister and his deputies. I have seen it happen at public meetings in the city of Toronto. Under the administration of the present deputy the police walk into a hockey match-I have not attended a professional hockey match since the war started- and ask some spectators for their registration cards. I read in the papers that the Toronto police are going all over the city requesting individuals to show their cards. They are trying to help the minister in his work.
Under the first system you had your registration card. I fail to see how that helped at all. There were returns made to orders of the house of prosecutions all over Canada for failure to register. They show a total of 150. Of that number 97 were in the city of Toronto and the remainder were in the military districts all over the country. The military districts have been changed. Take No. 10, Winnipeg; a large portion of that includes your constituency, Mr. Chairman, and part of northwest Ontario. Take No. 3, Kingston. That district includes the city of Ottawa. You find the same condition all across Canada. You find city of Toronto soldiers all over Canada in the air force. When I asked for a return in the house they could not tell me the number of men from 100-1644
Toronto who enlisted in the air force. The present Minister of National Defence for Air gave a return for the city of Ottawa. One was given for the city of Toronto but it did not go very far. One or two municipalities wrote me about it. I brought it up in 1940 and 1941.
Then we had the 1941 census, the national registration, and the plebiscite. What has happened to the returns in these cases? Are they all counted? They ought to be. Are they shown in the returns? So far as I can see, those returns might have been invaluable to the armed forces, but they were not used and we have now this system. Some use might have been made of them if they were available. We then have the unemployment insurance and the insurance books. Then you have the Canada Year Book which gives the results of the last war and last census. Then we have Mr. Lash on the radio. He was engaged on the radio to show that Ontario was falling down in recruiting as compared with Quebec. I have the greatest respect for all provinces. I have never raised the question of the differences between provinces in this committee. I believe in the principle of the old Cornish battle-cry, "all for each and each for all."
May I refer to table 7, which was printed in Hansard"! Regardless of what appears in that table in my opinion a battle royal has been going on here. The number missing, 300,000, has been referred to, and has been going up and down. It puts me in mind of the lost tribes of the children of Israel. We started census-taking away back in 1871 and it has been continued from that day on. The Canadian people are not mathematically minded. We have never been able to count the total number of people in this country, or where they came from. I know in one census half of one of the districts that I formerly represented in this house was left out altogether. Mistakes like that are made in counts all the time.
My comment is not against the present minister's department. I am trying to justify the necessity of utilizing all the money that has been spent on the census, registration * cards, by the wartime prices and trade board, the plebiscite, and all other bodies, and coordinate it all to give Canadians the rear facts. We should harmonize all the different counts and checks that have been made on man-power in this country since the war started. Where is all this information, and why is it not used? I was in the house before this department was created. I have raised the point before. I believe that each municipality should be entitled to know how many soldiers went to the front from that municipality. Men of the city from which I come
War Appropriation-Labour

have enlisted as far away as Vancouver and Victoria, and the city gets no credit for it. It does not want any credit, of course, except for helping to win the war. This is not a political matter; far from it. I have never tried to obtain any political advantage from it; I think that is a very poor argument at the present time, because as far as I can see the officials are doing their best, along the lines I have suggested. But we are back to conditions similar to those of 1066, when the Domesday book was drawn up, in the time of William the Conqueror. They counted the number of doctors, the number of workers, artisans, pigs, and all the rest of it, and put them down in that book. Now, in the fifth year of this war, all this money has been spent and we are not getting the results we should. We had several gentlemen use the radio in order further to becloud the situation, and others have done the same thing. I have read Hansard for the last few days, and this present debate reminds me of the battle of Dundee. I am not very good in the Scottish language, but according to the history books some say we won, some say they won and some say nobody won.
Surely there could be no objection to giving the figures of enlistments by provinces, by religions and all that sort of thing. It is done in the United States and in England and it is done here in connection with enlistments. When a man signs his attestation paper he says whether he is a Baptist, a Presbyterian, a member of the United Church or whatever he may be. The heads of some of these bodies have written me in this connection. As far as table 7 goes. I believe something should be done to harmonize that table with the various figures obtained through the registrations, the monthly pamphlets, the plebiscite, and so on. It may take a long time to do that. Only two or three years ago the present acting Prime Minister said he was changing the system followed in the records office in order to be able to give some of this information. When the war is over, each municipality will have to know how many enlisted from it in order that it may help the government in the postwar problems. I have had many municipalities of the province from which I come write me in connection with this matter, saying that from the records they cannot tell where their men are scattered, what has become of them or anything else.

The estimates now before the committee are among the most important to be considered by this house, because whatever the Labour department does affects the morale of a large section of the population of Canada. It also affects the relationship betweeen various

classes in the country, and the whole structure of national unity necessary both for victory and for a stable post-war period. Unfortunately I find that labour problems have been rather sidetracked in favour of a discussion of missing people, and the press have taken up this matter and made it a key problem. This house has become practically a missing persons bureau, with people wanting to find out exactly how many have not reported for military service. It has become a battle over figures. I hold no brief for men who do not report for army service, but I rather detect an attempt to slur the province of Quebec in this connection, and I say that is unworthy. Whom should we blame for the fact that certain people do not report? All parties in the past have carried on an agitation in Quebec, stating that our young men would not have to go to war.

They never said they
should not go to war.
No; that they would not have to go.
Speak for yourself, then.

Canadians work in similar plants at Cornwall. Why should those employed in the Quebec plants receive less than those employed in Ontario?
We are told, of course, that wages have to be low, because of competition. I have before me a report in the Montreal Gazette of a speech delivered by Mr. E. C. Fox, President of Canadian Cottons Limited, on March 8, 1944, in which he says:
If Canada is going to have a high standard of living, then she cannot expect her manufacturing industries to compete on level terms with countries of lower living standards.
By that he means that wages have to be kept very low if we are to be able to compete. That sort of attitude has to be changed. It is the kind of attitude which is not going to bring us a prosperous post-war period.
Then, what about competition from the United States? Before preparing my notes I had before me a file showing wages paid in textile mills at New Bedford, Massachusetts. There are many French Canadians down there, people who left their own province because they could get much more in wages than they could get here. They had a forty-hour week-although recently there has been a change to a forty-eight hour week. However they receive overtime for anything over the forty hours.
What other competition are we looking to? What about the far east-Japan? Qh, no; the world in the post-war period must never return to coolie wages. That is no reason for lower wages in Quebec. Not only are the wages low in the textile industry in our province, but an examination of the 1941 census showing average earnings in Quebec and Ontario for wage earners showed the following:

P.C. 1003 opens the door to company unions, and the unions will not be satisfied until they feel that company unions have been banned once and for all. I have before me an article which appeared in the Financial Post in reference to P.C. 1003, and which states:
Consistent with our democratic way of life-
It is peculiar how people can play with phrases.
-independent employees' associations are recognized and protected under the regulations.
I do not believe company unions have anything in common with the democratic way of life. And no one can tell me or anyone who has been in the labour movement for any length of time that a company union is something which the workers cry for as a baby cries for castoria; it is something imposed upon them'. P.C. 1003 permits lockouts in industries where there is no collective agreement. In the same article in the Financial Post we read:
An employer is only .restrained from locking out his employees if there is a collective agreement in force.
If there is not, he has the right to lock out his employees.
You are just quoting the opinion of an individual. It is like all your other stuff-just quotations from what somebody else has said.
I read this through, and I am sorry to have to say that I agree with quite a number of the things I find in this article.

My hon. friend claims to speak as a trade unionist. I should like to tell him that this order in council has the approval of the parent bodies of the largest labour organizations in Canada. I know the hon. member intends to send this speech back home, and I hope he will forgive me for interrupting. There is a definite penalty provided in the code for the fostering of company unions or what my hon. friend refers to as company unions. The mere fact that the Financial Post says a thing does not mean that it is true. This order is being administered by a board made up equally of men nominated by labour and by employers' organizations. I do not think my hon. friend speaks for the trade union movement in this country.

I have not considered myself as speaking for the trade union movement of this country, I am too modest for that.

War Appropriation-Labour
Any more than, you spoke for the Canadian people in 1941.

That is all right; there is no sense in getting hot under the collar about it. I congratulated the minister; I said it was an improvement on what we had before. I believe that an hon. member has the right to point out certain weaknesses. In the past we have had a long struggle for improvement and we have got improvement, but I think I have the right to point out certain weaknesses which exist. The interpretation given in the order to employees' organizations is too broad. I would say that it could include company unions.
There is the question of certification which I should like the minister to explain. Would it not be possible to arrange that in all factories where there are collective agreements there shall be automatic certification? That would avoid going through this procedure which can lead to confusion and which may be taken advantage of by certain employers. These are a few of the things I want to say about order 1003.
Then there is the problem of labour-management relations. I am afraid that here I shall have to be more critical than I have been about order 1003. The other day I received a booklet pointing out what labour-management committees have done in the United States and in Great Britain, but it could not say much about labour-management relations in Canada. We are in the fifth year of the war and there should be many labour-management committees throughout this country. We have heard a lot of talk about them, but there has been no move by the government to help organize these committees.
This affects not only production, which is important, but also lay-offs. I am not saying that lay-offs may not be necessary when changes in production are made, because they are. Because of war conditions a plant making one thing to-day may be asked to make another thing to-morrow. A shift in production must be made and a labour-management committee could discuss the problem. The workers would feel that they had been consulted and perhaps would be ready to go somewhere else if that were necessary.
Surely labour and management can get together to discuss ways and means of using their equipment for post-war production. They should be able to work out what they can produce instead of cannon and tanks. Labour people also have brains and they should have a chance to make proposals. That is why I say we should follow the example of other united nations. In Great Britain there are 4,000 committees in the metal industry alone,
and they have done wonders. In the United States many committees have been set up, but we have very little of that in Canada. Something more than pamphlets is needed here. It should be the task of this committee which has been reorganized to go to town in helping in the organization of these labour-management committees.
Before sitting down I should like to say a few words to which some hon. members may take exception. I think they should be said in fairness to the people of the city of Montreal, the people of the province of Quebec and the people of all Canada. In saying what I intend to say I do not want to minimize in any way the heroic efforts of the men in the armed forces and the tough job they are doing. I refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey), who is reported on page 2455 of Hansard as follows:
In the last three or four weeks I have seen, I frankly admit, only three Canadian cities, Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto, hut what I have seen in those cities is to me as alarming -as it is tragic. If I -may generalize from these local observations I would say that Canada at the moment is not so much a nation motivated by a full-out war effort, tout is on the other hand, it would seem, in many ways a nation enjoying the greatest prosperity in its history. These days appear to me to be as gilded and as giddy as those of 1929.
I think that is an unjust statement to make about the people of Montreal. Many people in Montreal live away from St. Catherine street and the centre of the city. Had the hon. member gone to see some of the huge war plants where men and women, young and old, work under conditions which are not the easiest; had he visited a night shift and seen men working who in some cases had not seen their families for days; had he visited a shell-filling plant or one of the acid-mixing rooms and seen people working under the most difficult of conditions; had he known how the people had subscribed to war loans, how they were living in poor homes, how they were giving their blood and doing everything they could, he would have arrived at a different conclusion.
Yes, the workers may drink a little more beer or whisky; for an extra glass of beer is appreciated by the working man after a hard day's work. But that by no means indicates prosperity. There is far from prosperity in Montreal at the present time, and I think the hon. gentleman should have lectured some of the members of his own party, especially a new recruit who had been given an honourable job under the government where as chairman of the national labour board he could have done something for

I did not want to make these remarks, but I was in Montreal over the week-end and I know that quite a number of people were insulted by the remarks that were made. Mr. Chairman, I
rise to a question of privilege in connection with a statement made in the house by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay as reported at page 2588 of Hmsard, where he quoted a statement made by M. Pare, registrar of military district F. M. Pare's statement was as follows:
It is absolutely untrue that, in Quebec district, only 9,000 out of 460,000 "callable" men have been called up, as was alleged iby Mr. John B. Diefenbaker, Progressive Conservative member for Lake Centre. In the first place, in our district, there are but 180,000 "callable" men, not 460,000.
The statement arises by reason of a misapprehension of the words that I used and their removal from the context. I never said that 460.000 "callable" men were in Quebec district F. I never said that only 9,000 men out of 460,000 "callable" men in Quebec district F were called up for service. What I did say is to be found at page 2497 of Hansard, and I feel that any misapprehension caused by failure to read the entire paragraph should now be removed. What I said was:
The number called for medical examination to January 31, 1944, was 1,449,417.
Then I paused to remark that I was not referring to call-ups for service at all but to call-ups for medical examination. I went on:
In other words, 469,942 have been called up for medical examination since June 23, 1943-
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): To January.
Mr. Diefenbaker: Up to the 31st of January, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury says. Here is how they called them up. They called up a total from the various military districts of the number I have given. In Quebec military district, division F, they called up 8-6 per cent of the total population, or, in that period of time, only 8,724 out of some 460,000 men.

My remarks were removed from their context. The 460,000 men referred, in round figures to the 469,942 called up for medical examination throughout Canada since June 23, 1943.
