(2)	Space and adequate play equipment.
(3)	Companionship.
(4)	Consistent routine.
(5)	Careful supervision of health.
I would suggest that there are women already who are working who do not come within the provisions of the various forms of insurance which are given to men. Women teachers and women nurses do not come under the employment insurance benefits which are open to men and I feel that a grave injustice is done to these women in that regard.
For those women who feel that they have not the ability or the education or the skill or the liking for other occupations, there is of course a very large demand that they should work at domestic service. But there again, in that field of women's work, I believe we have to do a great deal to make it attractive to them and to safeguard them. A little while ago I received an interesting letter from a young woman, who addressed her letter from the Y.W.C.A. in Edmonton, Alberta. It was a well written letter, such as would indicate that the writer was an intelligent and well educated girl. I should like to read the first two paragraphs of her letter:
Two or three of us who are in domestic work here are hoping to work up some interest in a union for domestics. We should greatly appreciate your advice.
I have been interested in this work for a number of years, though I have not been able to work at' it steadily. I have been working for some months as cook general at the home of Lieutenant-Governor J. C. Bowen and lost my position a few days ago immediately on their becoming aware of my union activities. I was given no notice.
That is not perhaps indicative of the usual way in which capable and good domestic servants are used by their employers, but it indicates that there is no protection in a case such as this for a young woman who has loyally and faithfully served her employer as a domestic servant, and who yet expresses the desire to belong to a union of her choice to protect her rights.
These women wish to protect their rights, hours of labour, pay, the length of time they should be given by way of notice before leaving employment, and so on. I would say there is great need that we should protect
women in domestic service. The committee to which I referred a little while ago, the subcommittee of the government's committee on reconstruction, has the following to say regarding the employment of women as domestic servants and in household work:
(1)	A standard of proficiency should be set by a training programme financed by the dominion and provincial governments. The cost of training should be borne by the government, but the student should carry her own living expenses with the help-if necessary-of government loans at low interest rates.
(2)	A signed agreement made between employer and employee, made through national selective service, would protect both by providing a definite statement regarding wages, termination of employment and other working conditions. Any dominion or provincial labour code should include household workers.
_ (3) Labour legislation should be amended to include household workers under the minimum wage acts and related legislation.
(4)	Occupational branches of social insurance should be open to household workers, that is, unemployment insurance, workmen's compensation.
(5)	An organized supply of trained part-time workers should be made available to fill the need for various types of household service. This kind of service is particularly required in homes of moderate income where it is impossible for the housewife wth several children to have full-time assistance.
I realize that the women of this country have not as yet formulated their wishes with regard to these particular problems, but I noticed in the Montreal Gazette, in March of this year that the women of Australia had been far ahead of their Canadian sisters in working out for themselves a certain code embodying their wishes and desires and the demands for which women in Australia will consistently fight until they are successful. I should like to commend the women of Australia for the progressive steps they have taken, and I only wish the women of Canada would see the wisdom of themselves doing something along the same line. From the Montreal Gazette of March 22 I quote the following:
An Australian women's conference here prepared a women's charter which they managed to compress into a mere 5,000 words, but it took them a long time to do it. Further compressed, here it is:
Woman as citizen:	No discrimination in
respect of the responsibilities and rights of men and women as citizens.
Mother and homemaker:	The indispensable
service rendered to the community by mothers demands special consideration of fullest maternity services, nursery schools and opportunity for creative work; and, as dependent economic status denies liberty, opportunity and justice to the homemaker, and that economic independence strengthens character, we recommend a personal endowment of a minimum of 30 shil-
War Appropriation-Labour

lings ($5.50) a week be -paid to her foy the commonwealth, operating on the same system as child endowment which shall continue.
Woman as voluntary worker to be recognized for her great contribution to the community, and have opportunities, and be given expert training in the social services that she may attain professional status.
Woman in the services be granted the same status, pay, dependents' allowance and other benefits and opportunities offered to men.
Woman in the country foe afforded facilities in rail transport, telegraph services, water conservation, special mobile health and baby care services.
Woman in public life to be given opportunity to go forward and stand as candidate for national and international delegations, legislative bodies, diplomatic posts, responsible administration, and as members of boards, and commissions, in order that their potential capabilities may be developed and utilized for the national good.
Woman as peacemaker:	The part women
have played in their country's struggle to win the war justifies that they foe given wide representation at international peace table.
I wish the women of Canada would urge that the same liberties and freedoms, the same justice be accorded to them in this country and that they, too, have the right to represent a part of Canada at the peace table when that happy time comes.
In what I have said to-night, I am of the opinion that were we to grant these further privileges and rights to the women of Canada, it would not mean -that they would wish the more to forsake the home. They would rather, I believe, feel that motherhood was their primary duty, and as long as marriage and motherhood was not the only avenue open fo them they would, I believe, embrace it with all the more love, feeling that they had chosen it because it was the thing that was nearest and dearest to their hearts. When women do have all the free pursuits of a great nation open to -them they will, I believe, become better citizens and, because of that, better mothers, and they will bring to the home the feelings of equality and devotion as the basis for happiness to a far greater degree than they do at the present time.
Before closing I would ask the Minister of Labour to indicate whether or not he is prepared to press the question of equal wages for equal work being made a part of the labour code and enforced in the country.

I am afraid my hon. friend is a little out of date. As a matter of fact, it was twelve months ago that I was chairman of the national war labour board, and while I was so acting the principle of equal pay for equal production was laid lown

by the board. That in itself was a revolution. I think we were the first free nation that laid down that principle.
What has been done about it?
A great deal has been done about it.
What, for example?

I am not going into the
45,000	cases that come before the board dealing with the employment of men and women in the industrial structure, but as minister I am saying this and it should be enough, for my hon. friend, that the principle was laid down by the national war labour board when I was chairman.
One or two examples will be enough.
I do not carry all these decisions around in my pocket. If my hon. friend is ever unfortunate enough to hold this portfolio he will find it rather difficult himself.
Has the government applied the principle in practice?

Not the government but the national war labour board. They are the people who adjudicate on the wage structure. No one knows that better than my hon. friend. Let me pay this tribute to the women. The other afternoon when introducing my estimates I said that without the assistance of the women we could not successfully wage the war. The contribution made by the women of Canada has been magnificent. When I point out that 1,043,000 women are engaged in the industrial structure and that the women in the armed forces number 32,000 and on the farm, 760,000, according to the figures of September last year, hon. members will get an idea of the part played by the women of this country.
As I pointed out before, I was in Great Britain late in 1942, and I vividly remember speaking to the general council of the British trade union congress. I made the observation that the women were doing a better job than the men, and I suppose that is instinctive. In the family circle the women will fight harder for the children than will the average man. Therefore, when the nation or state is in jeopardy it is instinctive that our womenfolk will fight just as valiantly, and perhaps a little more valiantly, for the survival of the race and the state. My hon. friend can rest assured that this government

and I think I can speak for every government in this country and every party in this House of

War Appropriation-Labour
Commons-have just as much interest, and might I say real interest, in the progressive affairs of the womenfolk of this great dominion as anyone else. What my hon. friend said is quite true. Basically, I suppose, it is'as old as history itself. Men chase the good-looking girls. That is instinctive. The most natural thing to do, I suppose, as my hon. friend pointed out is settle down and see that there will be someone here two thousand years from now to call this country Canada. That is as old as history itself.
I appreciate the constructive suggestions made by my hon. friend this evening. She can be sure that not only this government but, as I have said previously, every government, whether provincial or municipal, will share the same views as my hon. friend with reference to the rights of the womenfolk in this broad dominion.

I wish to ask one more question. The minister has stated that the national war labour board and the government acknowledged the principle of equal pay for equal work. What happens then when a group of women in a certain factory are not receiving equal pay for equal work? Must they bring their case before the national war labour board?

My hon. friend knows this as well as I do. There are ten war labour boards in this country. They are the boards that adjudicate on the question of wages, whether they be men or women for that matter. Any individual engaged in any civilian pursuit has the right as an individual to place her case before either the regional board or the central board. If my hon. friend were engaged in a civilian pursuit she would place her case before the regional board in Saskatchewan, since that is her own province, or if she were engaged in a national industry, before the national board. That is the machinery and that is the mechanics of it. While it is comparatively new, I suppose in the course of time it will develop a greater degree of supervision and will create working standards for men and women in this country.

I do not wish to delay the committee very long, but I have one or two questions I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. There have been special medical boards set up in certain industrial areas. I want the minister to pay attention to this inquiry because it is of paramount importance. Medical boards were set up in certain industrial areas outside the regional centres. They were established to examine men in the plants instead of their having to go to the regional district officers
or boards. As a result of the tapering off in certain industries recently, a great number of men were examined. In other words, as intimated by the hon. member for Vancouver South, there was a definite move on the part of the army to get thousands of men from industry into the army. That has been accomplished in part. Men hav been examined and moved into the army, men who have had complete mechanical training on all types of machine practice during the whole course of the war. A considerable number of these men have moved into the army because they were in certain types of industry which have tapered off their war production. Would the minister indicate what is to happen to these men who have been trained. It has cost industry a considerable amount to train them. They are going to be extremely useful because the Minister of Munitions and Supply has now demanded that certain types of munitions go back into peak production. Are these men to remain in the army, or will provision be made to have them go back to industry? The minister is probably aware of what I am saying and that it is correct. I wonder what it is proposed to do. Are these highly skilled men to remain in the army, or are they to be brought back to industry to help meet the requirements of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, of which he gave information a week ago? I should like some indication of what is to be done in this case.
There are special places where we have boards, places like St. Catharines, Fort William, and so on.
It has worked well.

Yes, I think it has. I assure my hon. friend that these highly skilled men such as toolmakers, coppersmiths, and so on-I could go on and give a list of these highly skilled trades that take many years to master; it takes years to make what we call a tradesman-will be moved to higher priority industry.
They are in the army now.

Let me come to that. If my hon. friend will wait for a moment I shall cover that. Do not forget that this is a mechanical war. I think my hon. friend and I sometimes make the mistake of thinking of this war in terms of the last war. This is an entirely different type of warfare. The number of mechanics required to-day is out of all proportion to the number required in the last war. That applies to the army, the navy and the air force. I can assure my
War Appropriation-Labour

hon. friend that any man with mechanical ability or training will find his proper niche in the three fighting forces of this country. As I pointed out earlier, these highly skilled tradesmen, such as toolmakers and coppersmiths, will be transferred to a higher priority industry. It takes many years to produce a toolmaker; but we are seeing to it that they are transferred to a higher priority industry.
I do not think my hon. friend was in the house this afternoon when I made the observation that we have a group of industrial engineers going through the industrial structure of Canada and working in cooperation with employers in an effort to comb out those industries in order to supply the necessary man-power for the fighting forces. There is nothing new about that. That policy has been undertaken in Great Britain for at least the last three years. Of course, they are under the influence of the blitz and the nearness of the enemy, and for that reason a much more rigorous and vigorous campaign is being carried on there than here. I can tell my hon. friend that due regard is being given to the needs of the industrial structure of this country. As I said earlier this evening, there is a limit to our man-power. It is my department that has to make the decision; and in this stage of the war I would say this, outside of those highly skilled trades the needs of the armed forces must, by the very nature of things, come first, unless in the light of future events another policy may seem more expeditious.

I wish to ask one more question. Then I am to gather from what the minister says that the very men who have been making munitions of war for four years and have become highly skilled and proficient are now to be taken from those industries and put in the army, navy or air force, and will remain there and that we shall have to go back and train other men or women to do exactly the same job and make exactly the same munitions as were being made in certain plants throughout this country before. I draw that deduction from what the minister says.

You are not going to draw that deduction from what the minister says. I am not going to let you get away with that. It is not as simple as that. We are not a gang of waifs and strays or trained seals.
Well,-
That is all right. Wait a moment. My hon. friend was somewhat vigorous in the question he put to me. I want to try not to be as vigorous as he wTas. v
You are talking about trained seals.

That is all right. We have a degree of common sense, I think, and that is the yardstick. The men who are going through these plants are sensible men. They are not like ships that pass in the night; they do not just pass through the plants without saying a word to anyone. They are talking to the management of these plants, sizing up conditions in the various industries across this country.
That is that side of it, but there are always two sides to a medal. At the present rate, for various reasons approximately sixty thousand men a year are being discharged from the armed forces, so that we shall have those sixty thousand men coming into our commercial, industrial and agricultural structure with these other men leaving the three important structures in the life of this dominion to take their places. That is the balance.
But only a small percentage of the men returning go back into industry, and they are not skilled.
I pointed out while my hon. friend was not in the house-
I was in the house all afternoon.

I think I mentioned
previously to-day that I could put 160,000 people at work to-morrow morning if I had them. There has been no serious difficulty up to the present in placing every man who has been discharged from the armed forces.
I will go further in that regard. We have a rehabilitation and training plan for men discharged from the armed forces. Notwithstanding the many thousands who have been discharged, up to this date-and I am speaking now from memory-only three thousand have availed themselves of the training facilities made available by the government, which is an indication that all the other tens of thousands have found their way through selective service back into the industrial structure.
It may be that the allowance offered them was not large enough.
I am not talking about that now; there will be a time and place to argue that matter. They have found their way back into the commercial, industrial and agricultural structure of this country.

straight. I do not think it is mimeographed; if my hon. friend will look at it he will see it is typewritten.

In case I may be told that I do not know what I am talking about, and that the minister is a former railwayman-probably he still belongs to his union-let me say that when I speak of railway employees I do know what I am talking about. In case that is denied, however, let me say that I hold in my hand the most serious railway publication printed on this continent, namely the "Railway Age",

War Appropriation-Labour
published in the United States. This is an old periodical, dating back to 1856, and I find in the recent issue of February 19, 1944, the following editorial respecting new employees and accidents:
Reports of recent accidents continue to emphasize the serious and frequently fatal results that come from mistakes made by new employees. Brakemen and firemen with less than a year's experience continue to prove, beyond any question, that a railroader cannot be made overnight, and that, regardless of the alertness and competence of these men, there is no substitute for experience in railroading.
This situation places an enlarged responsibility upon railway officers and older employees. Increased vigilance is demanded of them to prevent the new men from making tragic mistakes. They must keep everlastingly at the teaching of new men, acquainting them with the complexity of railway operation. They can never assume that a new man knows the railroad, merely because he has been over it several times.
The intimate knowledge of every switch, siding, station and signal that is so necessary to prevent accidents cannot be attained suddenly, and no one except older employees and supervisors make good this deficiency.
While there is much that railways can and should continue to do to meet their needs for competent labour, the final solution to the difficulty lies in the hands of selective service boards. The withdrawal of experienced manpower has reached an extent which cannot be corrected by makeshifts and expedients.
Note the word "expedients."
The selective service 'board which calmly told a railway in a vital area that a good man could be taught telegraphy and made a train dispatcher in six months presents a typical example, rather than an isolated case, of the sort of ineptitude

And mark that word.
*-that is ruining the railways' ability to maintain their vitally needed transportation.
I am pleased to quote this, because while it was printed in the United States, it deals with similar problems. The article goes on:
Perhaps the railways themselves have contributed to such misunderstanding on the part of those responsible for recruiting men. They have cooperated wholeheartedly with selective service authorities, and have given freely of their best officers and men to the battalions of the military railway service-perhaps inducing the opinion that they had plenty of personnel to spare. This cooperation is laudable-
And I agree with that.
-but it is now even more patriotic to resist the further depletion of the ranks of skilled railway labour.
I agree with that.
Colonel Johnson of the interstate commerce commission merits wholehearted cooperation from the railways in his efforts to awaken the authorities to the grave national danger in depleting railway forces 'below the point adequate to maintain the nation's war-time transportation.
And then on page 397:
B. & M. Advertises Against Man-power Losses.
Asserting that "you can't run as hazardous and as complicated a business as a railroad with a majority of green men," the Boston and Maine has begun what it terms an "out" in the open approach to the question of man-power deferment. Its answer to those who attack army-age trainmen for being out of uniform, and who charge them with being slackers, comes in the form of an advertisement which now is being run in all newspapers along B. & M. lines.
Entitled "Who says, 'You Can't Fight with a Lantern?"', the advertisement describes railroading as a "tricky business"-"where safe things to do are learned only 'by experience."
May I remind the minister that this is not a joke; it is a serious matter and this is not the time for him to laugh. The article continues:
For the benefit of the uninformed, the message points out that there are now 3,053 of the 16,000 regular B. & M. employees now in the armed services. Moreover, many of the younger men have sought their release from the railroad, asking that the draft board be notified to cancel their deferments. The railroad reply, it is explained, has been "no," because "if all of them went, it would mean that there'd be chaos-accidents, delays in moving the many important things for fighting men which are being manufactured in New' England's war plants."
Is that not what has been said by many hon. members in this house, especially by the member for Temiscouata. I continue:
The advertisement argues that "an experienced trainman on a passenger train isn't just a fellow who opens the door and yells 'Swampscott' and then waves a lantern". He must be familiar with scores of rules, signals and train schedules, that trains can speed with precision and safety. Nor can the experienced trainman on a speeding freight train, who performs his task with unnecessary delay and without accident, be spared. "It's far too important a job to trust entirely to inexperienced men, and it's a job that must have the alertness and the quick judgment of seasoned employees."
_ So, requests the Boston and Maine, "the next time you see one of our younger employees doing his most important part in the fight to win the war, we ask that you ponder a bit before you say, or think-slacker".	"He's in fighting
uniform right here at home", says the railroad.
I have this large file containing letters between Mr. Coleman and the Minister of Labour. It starts with a letter from Mr. D. C. Coleman and Mr. Vaughan, the presidents of the two large railways, dated March 31, 1943, addressed to the Minister of Labour, and reading as follows:
Since the outbreak of war in September, 1939, there has been a steady and progressive decrease in the number of trained personnel available for essential railway occupational classifications The calling up of men for military service irrespective of the essentiality of their occupations and the exercise by numerous employees
War Appropriation-Labour

of the right to leave railway service to volunteer for the armed forces have combined to produce in railway ranks a shortage of qualified manpower that has assumed serious proportions.
Is that not what the member for Temis-couata has said repeatedly This is over the signatures of the presidents of both the large railroads. The letter continues:
Efforts of the railways to train replacements have only partially alleviated this condition and it is now clear that any further aggravation of the situation will have such effect upon the operating efficiency of the railways as may in the near future curtail or render impossible maintenance of certain railway services essential to the national war effort.
With a view to formulating a practicable and comprehensive plan to ensure the continued operation of rail transportation services at the maximum efficiency for the duration of the war, representatives of the railways conferred on several recent occasions with officials of the national selective service, mobilization section, at Ottawa. The suggestions made by the railways were sympathetically received and officials of the national selective service, mobilization section, cooperated in every way possible. They pointed out, however, that a permanent solution of this very urgent problem involves a radical departure from the current governmental manpower policy and suggested that the factual data presented to them together with the railways' recommendations thereon should be placed before the government for its consideration and decision.
The railroads were trying to keep their men, and it was a departure from the government policy to take men from the railroads.
The letter continues:
Pursuant to this suggestion there are submitted herewith analytical statements designed to illustrate the magnitude of the existing shortage in essential occupational classifications and the crippling additional drain on railway manpower the current system of call up for compulsory military service will inevitably entail.
At February 28, 1913, there were 24,832 employees of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways in the armed forces of Canada serving at home or abroad or in the merchant navy. Of this number a substantial proportion were engaged prior to enlistment or call in essential occupational classifications. In addition, 33,406 employees now actively engaged in railway work are in the age groups subject to compulsory military call, of whom 21,417 are in essential occupations, and the remainder must be replaced if and when called.
It is the considered view of the railways that any further loss of employees in the essential occupational classifications cannot be sustained without a serious and perhaps disastrous impairment of vital transportation services, and that this threat of a further drain on their already limited man-power should be removed once and for all by governmental action. It is, therefore, respectfully suggested that the government should adopt with the utmost dispatch a policy that will ensure definite deferments of compulsory military service for all railway employees engaged in essential occupational classifications.
The loss of man-power to the armed forces, however, is only one aspect of the situation.
[Mr. Pouliot.l
Not only have the railways been faced with the problem of securing suitable replacements for those in military service but owing to the unprecedented war-time demands for transportation they have also had to secure and train large numbers of new employees. Some conception of the magnitude of this task may be gathered from the fact that in 1942 the average number of employees in both the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific totalled 150,623 as compared with 123,671 in 1939, an increase of 26,952 or 21-8 per cent. This compares with an increase of 90-9 per cent in traffic in the same period as measured by the increase in the combined traffic units of the two railways.
Another factor which has contributed to the difficulties attendant upon the maintenance of tile high standard of efficiency of Canadian railways during war time is the strain placed upon experienced employees as a result of having to work side by side with inexperienced employees. This places upon the experienced men additions responsibility especially during the training perod when the new employees are unfamiliar with their duties. Employees such as locomotive engineers, locomotive firemen, conductors, trainmen, yard switching forces, telegraphers, track forces and others, upon whom the safe operation of trains depends, are thus required to labour under most trying conditions. The railways view with increasing concern the consequent impairment, at this time of heavy wartime traffic, in the efficiency of these experienced and essential employees.
Mark that.
The railways view with increasing concern the consequent impairment, at this time of heavy war-time traffic, in the efficiency of these experienced and essential employees.
It goes on:
In addition to the loss of experienced men in the essential occupational classifications the railways have sustained a further depletion in qualified personnel due to the loan to the government either on a full-time or part-time basis of a substantial number of officers and other employees for special war work, and to the transfer of a large number of officers and skilled men to munitions work. These officers and men have been made available regardless of the inconvenience to the railways.
The urgent need for conservation and utilization to the fullest degree of the existing supply of available man-power is recognized by the railways and every effort in that direction has been consistently made since the outbreak of hostilities. A number of men physically fit and willing to continue working are being retained in service after reaching normal retirement age, and likewise in some cases retired employees are being reemployed for the duration. The hours of service in essential occupational classifications have in many instances been extended and certain positions usually reserved for men are now being filled by women. It is the intention to- extend these practices as conditions permit. As far as possible the railways are prepared to further extend the transfer of employees to territories where due to fluctuation of traffic temporary shortages exist. However, with the uncertainties involved in traffic fluctuation as between one territory and another and the man-power situation in its present critical stage, the transfer of employees, except as a temporary expedient to meet some particular local emergency, no longer offers the

War Appropriation-Labour
opportunity for full utilization of man-power that it did in the first few months of the war.
Railway officers in conjunction with representatives of the employees are constantly exploring every possible means of making the fullest use of all available man-power in the essential occupational classifications.
The factual data contained in the attached analytical statements have been prepared with the object of presenting a clear picture of the man-power situation of the steam lines of each railway, with separate statements for each of their affiliated activities. Employees have been divided into two classifications: namely, essential occupations and other occupations.
The railways are of the opinion, as already indicated, that in the interests of the national war effort the continued drain on essential railway man-power should be immediately and effectively stopped. Railway employees now serving with the armed services in Canada should be given leave to return to their former essential employment if they so desire.
It is impossible to get them out of the army. Moreover, they are taken from the railway and brought into the army, but when a request is made to get them out of the army and back to the railways it is impossible to get them out.
It goes on:
The only workable and practicable solution of the problem appears to be the adoption of a governmental policy in respect to compulsory military service that will ensure automatic deferment of calls of all railway employees engaged in essential occupational classifications on March 31, 1943.
In view of the seriousness of the situation and the urgent need for remedial action, it is respectfully requested that this matter be dealt with as promptly as possible.
Yours truly,
R. C. Vaughan, Chairman and President, Canadian National Railways.
D. C. Coleman, President,
Canadian Pacific Railway Co.
This letter gives matter for thought. The Minister of Labour then took the right course. He sent a copy of this letter to the three defence ministers. There was an acknowledgement from the minister for the navy, some correspondence from the air ministry, and a memorandum from the Minister of National Defence. Here is what the navy minister had to say in reply, on April 14. I shall not read it all because I have not much time. I shall read a paragraph. If the minister wants the rest put on Hansard I shall be glad to do so. This is what the navy minister had to say:
It is suggested that your department should set out definitely what are considered to be essential services, and instructions could then be issued to the armed forces to the effect that no men employed in any of these occupations shall be taken into the services. As far as the naval service is concerned, any men applying for entry into the service, _ when formerly engaged in farming, fishing, mining, lumbering,
et cetera, are to be fully questioned, and if it appears likely that they will ever need leave to return to their previous occupation, they will not be entered in the service. Furthermore, any men released from the navy to return to their former essential occupation will be discharged, and not reenrolled unless there is a change in the general situation.
If it is desired I shall consider whether instructions shall be issued to the effect that no railway men shall be enrolled in the naval service, and that railway men now in the service may be discharged to resume their former occupation.
Very good. 1 would not have thought the navy minister would have written, a letter like that about this matter to the Minister of Labour. It is a good letter. Now let us see what the minister for air had to say. In the first place, he replied on April 12 that the suggestion was being explored. In view of the fact that the average age of air force personnel is approximately twenty-three years, ft is not anticipated that many would fall into the category mentioned in the above letter from the two railroads. Under the new policy now being put forward for the minister's approval, any particular individuals required by the railroad and whose services can be spared will be eligible for discharge to return to civil employment.
That is very good. Now let us see what the Minister of National Defence wrote. He sent the Minister of Labour a memorandum, dated April 26, which reads as follows:
I have your letter of April 6, concerning man-power demands of the railways. I am in general agreement with the terms of your reply to the presidents of the two railway companies but wish to add the following comments.
Demands for exemption of essential workers are becoming daily progressively more numerous. We have discussed miners; the requests of fishermen, railroad men, teachers et al are put forward.
But the point is that, as you know, machinery already exists for postponement of essential workers (section 10 (8) N.S.S. Mob. Regs.).
That is the mobilization regulations. It goes on:
Regarding the suggestion in your penultimate paragraph concerning the setting up of a board: I myself do not see any need for a special board for railway men or any other occupation. Your mobilization boards can dispose of these questions pretty soundly if the evidence is placed before them. In any case, if you have some technical body to advise these boards



War Appropriation-Labour
regarding railway applications, such a body would not be complete without having among its members a representative of national selective service and a representative of the district officer commanding as well; otherwise the board would be entirely one-sided.
I fully recognize the importance of the railroad problem, but I very much doubt whether the army has drawn disproportionately upon the railroads for man-power. The fact that there are still 33,406 employees subject to call indicates that the mobilization boards are acting with due consideration of the transportation demands.
As regards effecting a return to the railroads of ex-employees now in the army, I must point out that personnel in the army here constitute potential reserves to assist in the maintenance of the army programme overseas and it would for that reason be detrimental to the success of that programme to sanction the release of personnel.
What programme? The army programme overseas, precisely the commitments that the Minister of National Defence made while he was in England-what I spoke of this afternoon.
Recognition must also be given to the fact that such personnel have received army training costing time and money and, furthermore, the army is now organizing railway troops for overseas.	[DOT]

May I add this further word purely by way of suggestion because it is out of my "line of country".

Respecting railway employees now in war service: I am led to believe-
1.	That most of the former employees now in tile armed forces come from the casual or parttime employees of the railroads, and
2.	that a substantial proportion of the 25,000 former employees now in war service are from the marine divisions of the companies and serving in the R.C.N. or mercantile marine.
"I am led to believe." Who told him that? What is the proof? It is signed J. L. Ralston. This is the letter of a jingo, and I have read enough to make the mouth of every member water and to make every member anxious to get the whole story. I thought the ministers

for the navy and the air were at one with the Minister of National Defence in insisting upon getting men from the railways into the army, but it is not that. Their letters are most reasonable; the only unreasonable letter comes from the head of the Department of National Defence, and that was written last year. Here is the answer that was sent before by the Minister of Labour to the heads of the railways:
I have before me your joint letter of March 31, which was presented in person by Messrs. F. W. Edge and H. D. Brydone-Jack, relative to the man-power situation as it affects the railways.
The problem of the man-power situation as it affects the two major employers composed of the railway systems of Canada is a matter which has been giving the department great concern. We have been aware of your difficulties through reports we have been receiving from our employment offices across Canada. Since the mobilization activity was taken over by the Department of Labour, we have been giving some study to the question of postponements from service for employees in "key" positions. For these reasons I was very glad indeed to have the opportunity of discussing the situation with your chief personnel officials.
I feel that it will not be out of place for me to, at this time, express my keen appreciation of the work the railway companies are doing and despite the considerable expansion in personnel, with a minimum of labour relations difficulties. Many of the labour policies of the government are made possible by the fact that this is so. I wish to go on record and thank you and your officials.
Coming to the question of mobilization of railway employees, we stand ready to give you every possible cooperation in this regard, and the representations will ibe given most careful study.
There are one or two brief comments I will make at this time.
In the classification of essential positions there are a few occupations which might, in the minds of the members of the mobilization boards, be doubtful. Those of "helpers"; "assistants"; "coal men"; "instrument men"; "work equipment firemen"; "section men" and possibly waiters on dining cars.
Your officials know your requirements better than we do, of course, but it does seem, wise at this time to explain that we are terribly short ot men for the armed forces.
The second point I wish to make is that in respect to getting new employees which you mention on page 2 of your letter, I would like you to feel that the full resources of the chain of employment offices across Canada are available to yon.
The third point I would wish to make is the question of identifying "essential men in essential occupations". Your officials stated that, while section men were listed, it was not the intention that all section men be considered as essential. How are we to identify the essential men from the non-essential? It did occur to me that a board composed of officials of the railways and possibly representatives of the labour organizations might be set up and doubtful cases could be referred to this board.
The last point I would mention at this time is the question of allowing men to return to

War Appropriation-Labour
their occupations who are already in the armed forces. There was some suggestion that older men now in the armed forces be exchanged for younger men in railway service. This idea, if workable, appeals to me; however I will confer with my colleagues who have the responsibility for the armed forces, in respect of this particular point.
Yours sincerely,
Humphrey Mitchell.
"This idea, if workable". The Minister of Labour was reasonable. The only one who spoke like a jingo was the Minister of National Defence. Copies of this letter were sent to the three defence ministers.
I have nothing to withdraw from the praise I have given the minister. I have said that, and I am in full sympathy with him. I think he has the treatment of a dog from the government. It is most unfair to put that responsibility on him, to hear complaints that come from your left, sir, when we know very well that the Minister of Labour does his very best to settle the matter in an amicable way, in a way that would not prejudice the country. It is just because we have one man who has no Canadian feeling, who has priority over his colleague, that it is impossible for him to do his job. "VVe see letters written by two men who are not supposed to be disciples of any nationalist in the province of Quebec or anywhere else, two men who are highly considered by the government, men who have been praised by the veterans themselves.
Why are we complaining so much and fighting the cause of the employees as we have been fighting the cause of the farmers? Why are the brotherhoods and unions dumb now? Why do the unions not do their duty in fighting this case as we do not only on behalf of the men, but on behalf of the railways? I do not know. I have no consideration at all for the leaders of brotherhoods who do not do their duty by fighting for the men and by fighting for the railways, as the chiefs of the railways themselves have done. To-day we poor people have to do that. How many times did I say in the house last year, the year before and in 1941, exactly what is said by both Mr. Vaughan and Mr. Coleman in their letter written last year to the minister? I have never seen that letter before. Is it not a justification of what I have been saying here in the house, justification to which there is no reply at all? I have been doing my duty. I have been fighting for the railways and sometimes I have been abused. I have been called a bad Canadian. I have been told that I do not understand the duty of the country to move reinforcements overseas all the time at the expense of the railways. It was not so long ago-it was yesterday or 100-166J
the day before-that we saw a dispatch in the press to the effect that in Australia manpower had reached rock bottom, that there was no more man-power. It is enough to listen to the letter written by the heads of the railways, men who are in an independent position to speak about this very matter. Then, due to the suggestions-I will say "suggestions"-made by the Department of National Defence there are men who had a month's training, who were brought from the railway to the army where they are rendering much less service than they could render in the railway business. Is that good government? I sympathize with the Minister of Labour. Someone forced his hand; and I deeply regret the importance that is given to the imperialists. I regret it the more because the Minister of Labour has judged the situation as a former railway man. He has understood it and he has put the facts before the war minister.
According to democracy we must have the rule of the majority. In that case they were two against one. They should have decided according to the decision of the two and the one should have been left aside, because the country should not be responsible for the dangerous commitments that he has made in London. They should be disapproved and he should be fired. That is what I have said many times. I cannot stand for it. Here I have as a testimonial two witnesses, the two heads of the two largest railways in this country.

I think I should say just a couple of words, not in full reply to my hon. friend. He spoke for forty minutes; I expect to speak for just a couple of minutes.
There is nothing unusual about the letter written by the railroads to myself in connection with the labour situation of these important undertakings. I suppose not a day goes by but what I get a letter couched in a similar vein. There is nothing new in a difference of opinion between individuals; that is why this House of Commons exists. But I wish to say this, Mr. Chairman: if everybody had their Way about the withdrawal of men from the armed forces we would not have any armed forces. Let us be clear about that. Again, we have set up the machinery between the railroads of this country and the Department of Labour in order that there might be an orderly withdrawal of man-power from the industry that is necessary under the present conditions.
Notwithstanding what is being said at this very moment, the railroads are moving more freight this very day than they have ever moved in the history of this country. Why
War Appropriation-Labour

are they moving that freight? In the great majority of cases because there is a war on across the Atlantic, because they are supplying the forces that are engaged in this conflict. I want to pay just this tribute to the two main railroad systems of this dominion, a tribute to both the management and employees on the contribution they are rendering at the present time. It is a difficult situation; of course it is. Everything is difficult in war time. There is not an industry in this country that is not going through a difficult period. When I say, "industry" I mean industry in its oroadest sense. It includes the farmers and :hose in commercial life. But it can be truthfully said, notwithstanding the criticism offered by my hon. friend-and I do not have any objection to that-that the railroads and their employees have carried on in what I might term a magnificent way, along with all the other industries; and whether we like it or not, this tightness in the man-power situation will continue until Hitler and that man in the Pacific are defeated.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say just a few words before this item is carried. I would not have risen at this time had not the hon. the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) stated on May 1 that a man who works on the farm has only to state that fact in order to obtain a postponement automatically. It is not as simple as that. In the first place, applicants must state the facts in an affidavit, and those who have been granted a postponement are told a, few months later that such postponements are no longer valid, and that they must file a new application.
We are told that postponements for farm work are readily granted. I know that such is not always the case. Besides, here is what the minister said on April 28 last, as reported on page 2445 of Hansard. I quote:
We are now finding it more difficult to fill the army requisitions- As the war progresses it is evident that wk. will soon 'have to rely largely upon those at present deferred and the young men coming of age.
And the minister placed on Hansard, at page 2452, table No. 9 from which I take the following figures. From March 20, 1941 to March 31, 1944, 245,443 applications for postponement filed by agricultural workers have been examined; out of that number, there were on the same date, that is on March 31 last, 145,529 postponements still valid. What about the other 100,000 applications which include the postponement applications that were denied and the applications for renewal which were not granted? Therefore,

less than three-fifths of the postponements for which applications were made are now valid. This proves conclusively that it is not so easy as he has intimated for farm workers to obtain a postponement.
Now I wish to say a word in regard to the order which was signed on January 28 last and in regard to the Employer's Guide published at the same time, which require every employer to report to the registrar any of his employees who are not in good standing under the mobilization act. This order and these regulations are inhuman, for they compel a brother to report his brother, a father to report his son. The employer is compelled to play an odious part, and if he fails to do so, he is liable, upon summary conviction, to a fine of not less than $25 but not exceeding $1,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years and a day, or to both fine and imprisonment.
I say that this order and these regulations must be repealed because they are antisocial and inhuman.
Mr. Chairman, we cannot be misled any longer, we have overseas conscription in disguise. On March 6. 1944, the government, in reply to a question asked by a member of this house, stated that men who had been called up for home defence, and who had not volunteered for overseas service, were sent to Newfoundland (including Labrador), to the British West Indies, to Bermuda, to Alaska, including Kiska. This is quite clear to anyone with an open mind.
Why does not the minister say to the house and to the country that the man-power pool is being depleted and that he is endeavouring by every possible means to attract men to the armed services?

In order to complete the record concerning the treatment of railway employees under the mobilization act, I wish to add something to what has been said by the hon. member for Temiscouata. The hon. gentleman has related the first chapter of the story; I should like to take a few minutes to relate the last chapter, which from the point of view of the railways and the railway employees is the most important.
I may preface what I have to say by stating that until the presidents of the two railways made representations in writing to the Minister of Labour, as related by the hon. member for Temiscouata, there was no central office of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or the Canadian National Railways organized to ask for postponements for rail-

War Appropriation-Labour
way employees called up for military service. Circular letters had been sent by the Canadian National Railways to district officers from one end of the country to the other, asking them to support applications for postponement when the men called up were considered essential in the operation of the railway. As might be expected, with several divisions and many more subdivisions, there was no uniformity in the interpretation of such essentiality on the part of local or district railway officials. As a result, in some districts railway employees who made application for postponement had their applications endorsed by their superior officers, while in other districts the superior officers would consider people employed at the same work as nonessential. So that dissatisfaction among the railway employees came to the attention of the heads of the railways, and representations were made to the Minister of Labour.
As a result of those representations, national selective service mobilization regulations were given an interpretation, and on June 14, 1943, circular memorandum No. 858 was forwarded to all chairmen and registrars. It has to do with applications for postponements by railroad transportation employees engaged by the Canadian National Railways or the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and the consideration thereof, pursuant to subsections 7, 8 and 10 of section 10 of the regulations. In order to bring about uniformity and afford the railways some relief, the Department of Labour recognized fhe necessity of giving consideration to employees who were essential in the operation of the railways, instructed the registrars and officials of the mobilization boards to give consideration to representations made on behalf of the employees by representatives of the railways, and for that purpose asked the two railways to set up a committee of responsible men who would pass upon the applications and decide as to the essentiality of the applicants in the operation of the railways. As a result, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company nominated Mr. Brydon-Jack, acting manager of the department of personnel, and the Canadian National Railways nominated Mr. Frederick W. Edge, director of labour relations.
This regulation was put into effect on June 14 and became operative on July 1, 1943. From that date to December 31, 1943, some 2,807 employees of the Canadian National Railways who were called up made application for deferment because they thought their employment was essential. Their applications were passed upon by Mr. Edge and the other members of the committee, and of all those
applications for deferment only sixty-eight were not approved by the committee because those men were not considered so essential that they could not be replaced by men not of military age or not subject to military call. This indicates that the new interpretation placed upon the mobilization regulations and the centralization of the consideration to be given by the railways have worked out very satisfactorily at least as far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned. I have not the figures for the period from January 1 to date, but I have been informed that the same proportion of applications have been approved. So that since July 1, 1943, relations between the Department of Labour and the two great railway systems of Canada have been most cordial, and applications for deferment for employees of military-age who were considered essential in the operation of the railways have been approved by the board.

After sitting here for a number of days listening to the discussion that has taken place, I have finally grasped something of the enormous task confronting the Minister of Labour, and at this late hour I have no wish to delay further the passing of this item. I should like, however, to mention a few matters to the minister. I am quite prepared to admit that I know very little about his problems and those of labour in the large industrial centres, though, as I say, I have come to realize that those problems must be enormous. But I do wish to draw to his attention the fact that the selective service board does not seem to function to the best advantage in the smaller centres. I shall not go into detail or belabour the point to any great extent, but shall mention only a few cases to show that it is not working satisfactorily in the smaller places.
I have in mind a man in my constituency. This man is beyond military age, and yet he is anxious to do *whatever he can. For over a year he has been in correspondence with the national selective service board, but that man still has not had satisfactory placement. Then I know of a young woman who had been in an egg-candling plant. After she had been in that plant for a considerable length of time the work slackened off. She then was laid off for the time being. As a young married woman she proceeded to attend to her household duties. Later on, the manager of the plant asked to have her return to work. She left her home at seven o'clock in the morning, and at one o'clock in the afternoon the selective service officials in that city had not yet prepared the necessary authoriza-
War Appropriation-Labour

tion for her to resume work in the plant in which she had been working formerly. I could mention quite a number of cases like that where men and women have suffered the loss of hours of work, through seemingly unneees-sarjr red tape. The loss would be great, if totalled.
Another matter I would draw to the minister's attention is unemployment insurance. In some parts this, too, does not work to the satisfaction of the people in the smaller communities. I shall give one or two examples. For instance, an elevator man receiving only a very small wage contributes to unemployment insurance. He has a family to take care of. Then the elevator is closed down, and he has no further possibility of earning money for several months, until the next crop season comes along. If that man accepts the terms laid down by the unemployment insurance officials under which he must accept employment at some other place, very often he would be working at a rate of pay which would leave nothing for him or his family, after the necessary amounts for living expenses away from home were deducted.
Some other cases were drawn to my attention during the Easter recess. People who had been working at comparatively small wages could not take advantage of the unemployment insurance to which they had contributed, when they were laid off for short periods of time.
I draw these points to the attention of the minister, realizing that his problems are great. The industrial and larger centres may have a more orderly way of working out the details, but I must point out to him that in the smaller centres it is far from satisfactory.

I should like to ask a question with regard to men who had training and the necessary experience in the air force who rose to the rank of commissioned officer and then were found unfit for further operational duties, after which they were eased out of the force. The minister will remember that on Tuesday the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked what was being done with commissioned officers who were found medically unfit. I wondered if any provision is being made under this item to give men such as these training which will enable them to fit into other activities.

Provision is made under the rehabilitation section, and men discharged from the armed forces can receive training under this plan.
Mr. BLACIvMORE:	Suppose an officer
discharged from one of the armed forces decides to enter one of these schools; would he then be exempt from call-up while in the school?
Yes, absolutely.

I was talking to-day with some boys who are greatly disturbed about the whole situation. It looked to them that the only course which would be open to them would be to enter some other activity in life, wait a few days and then be called into the armed forces and have to go through
all the drudgery and misery which an ordinary recruit goes through and then probably not be able to rise to the rank of sergeant. They would thus suffer loss of money and loss of dignity and prestige.
If a man has been discharged medically unfit from the army he has a right to enter a training class.
I am thinking particularly of the air force.

From the army, navy or air force. There is nothing undignified in being a private in the army, navy or air force.
I was one myself in the navy during the last war.

Did you go through it
twice?
I was there all the time, but there is nothing undignified in being a private.

What is bothering these boys is the possibility of having to go through it all again. They have gone through the misery of being a private once and they rose to the commissioned ranks. They are faced with the possibility of having to go through it all again. That sort of thing does not make these boys feel very good and I was just wondering if there is not some way out.	'

I cannot imagine a situation developing such as that to which my hon. friend refers. If a man is discharged as medically unfit from one of the services I would think he is out of that service. As I said earlier this evening, we do not know how this war is going to develop or what may be necessary a year from now. I should not like to project my thought so far into the future. As I said before, however, I cannot conceive, once a man is medically unfit and discharged from the forces, that he will be called back again; that is under normal circumstances.

The minister will
remember that when the matter was being discussed on Tuesday the question arose of a man being colour-blind to an extent to render him unfit for operational flights. That might result in his discharge, but it would not unfit him for duty in the army, and the result is he would be called up as soon as he got out of the air force.

I would say that it is every man to his own last. I am running the Department of Labour, not the air force, navy or army. They have their own departments to worry about. Giving my own opinion only, I - can see many reasons why a man might

become unfit to operate an aeroplane or carry out some specialized task in any one of the services, although he might be perfectly efficient for some other job. I think I referred to seasickness the other day. I suffered from it myself and I know what it is like. I can quite understand where a man would be discharged from the navy because he could not stand the motion of ships. There are many admirals in the British and other navies who suffer from seasickness. If such a man were discharged from the navy he might prove to be A1 for the air force or the army.

The difficulty arises from the fact that he may have risen in the ranks beyond the rank of sergeant. Then he is discharged and he finds he has to start all over again. I wonder if there is not some course of training he could take so that he would not have to go through that drudgery again.

I have tried to be as plain as I possibly can. We have to train them.

I should like to have a little information with respect to this item. How many of these vocational training schools have been established, particularly in the west? How many are taking courses at the present time? There seems to be some misunderstanding with respect to these courses. I have had some correspondence with the superintendent of vocational training in Ottawa and also with the district rehabilitation board at Regina. Under the arrangements made with the man who took on the job of giving this training, provision was made for eight men. Six turned up to take the course, with the understanding that when they had completed a four months' course they would be given some assistance in becoming established and starting up. The course was in shoemaking, harness-making and repairing.
